_comment: WHERE a scene happens. The third data table, alongside scene-styles.json (how it is drawn)
and scene-activities.json (what the children are doing), and split out for the same reason:
the weekly run must be able to produce a different picture every week without anybody
editing Python.
`season` is a list of months (1-12) the setting suits. The weekly picker keeps only the
settings that match the current month, so a snowy hill does not turn up in July. Every
setting must belong to at least one month and the union must cover all twelve, or some week
of the year has nothing to draw; tools/scene-week.py checks that and refuses rather than
quietly falling back to a default nobody chose.
`crowd` is the second half of the prompt and it is what makes a search-and-find picture one
at all: the mechanic is finding yourself AMONG many figures, so a setting with three people
in it is a portrait, not a game. Keep these dense.
NOTHING HOUSEHOLD-SPECIFIC GOES IN HERE. These strings are sent verbatim to a hosted model.
No name, no age, no address, no school, no real place the family goes — build-plan §3.1, and
prompt_guard.enforce reads the assembled prompt and will refuse anyway. A setting is a GENRE
of place ('a mountain lake in late summer'), never this family's actual weekend.
FOUR FANTASY SETTINGS were added 2026-09-10, asked for by name: 'there's, like, a fantasy
scene, let's display like a night scene, a frozen theme... could do another one that's Narnia
themed, because [the eldest]'s been really into that.'
THEY ARE THEMES, NOT TITLES, and that is deliberate rather than timid. Naming Elsa and Anna,
or Narnia, does three things wrong at once. They are trademarked characters, so a hosted image
model either refuses them or drifts towards a half-remembered likeness; the household's own
children would then be competing with somebody else's characters for the viewer's attention;
and this picture is NAVIGATION — a child finds herself in it and taps herself — so a costume
that makes her look like a film character is working directly against the one job the image
has. `ice-palace` is the ice palace and `lamppost-wood` is the snowy wood with the lamp-post
and the castle on the hill. Everything that made the child ask for them is in the setting.
The children in them are still the children.

`tags` is the activity filter's vocabulary (scene-activities.json `settings`: beach, forest, lake, meadow, mountain, park, river). An empty list means 'no outdoor kind' — activities tagged to a place are skipped and the untagged ones remain. Added 2026-09-13 when a sledge turned up on green hills: gen-scene had the filter and scene-week never fed it.

settings._comment: Asked for 2026-10-04 for the week of the school book fair, with each child's own costume choice. Season [] on purpose: never drawn by the timer (the costumes are this year's), only by --setting.
settings.setting: a school library turned into a Halloween book fair, long folding tables piled with brightly coloured picture books and chapter books, tall spinning wire racks of paperbacks, strings of orange and purple paper bats and paper pumpkin garlands across the shelves, carved jack-o'-lanterns grinning on the end of each table, a reading tent made from a big cardboard castle draped with cotton-wool cobwebs, bean bags on a rug, warm late-afternoon light through tall classroom windows

settings.wardrobe: Halloween costumes, a different one each. Child 1 is dressed as a clever young witch from a boarding-school story — a long black school robe open over a grey knitted jumper, white collared shirt, a red-and-gold striped tie and a grey pleated skirt, a thin wooden wand in one hand and a tall stack of heavy books hugged in the other arm; no hat; her own long wavy hair loose exactly as it always is. Child 2 is dressed as a big fluffy ginger cat — a soft orange-ginger furry costume with darker ginger stripes, a fat bottle-brush tail, and a headband of pointed ginger cat ears worn on top of her own loose long hair, whiskers and a little pink nose drawn on her cheeks in face paint; no hood and no mask. Child 3 is dressed as a wizard king — a small shiny gold crown sitting on top of his blond fringe, a long royal-purple velvet cape with a white fluffy trim and little gold stars sewn on it, and a wooden wand with a gold star on its tip held up high.

settings.crowd: skaters on the frozen fountain pool, a reindeer in harness, small snow-figures with carrot noses, a woman selling hot drinks from a cart, lanterns on posts, a robin on a frost-covered branch, children dragging sledges, a cat asleep on a warm stone
settings.wardrobe: fur-trimmed winter capes and embroidered boots in jewel colours, as if they were guests at the palace rather than visitors to it.

story._note: CHRONOLOGICAL reading order: each moment's `through` is the point in the series by which a reader has met it (a float, so 1.5 means book one finished and book two started). read_through is how far THIS household has read, and it is household data, so the committed value is the lowest that keeps the spoiler selftest meaningful. Set yours in your own copy; the later moments are already here and inert until it passes them.

settings._comment: Asked for 2026-10-12, the day the household went swimming (BACKLOG 4.11, option 2). Season [] on purpose and enforced by check_tables: a swimwear picture is only ever drawn because an adult forced it with --setting, never by the timer. `swimwear` swaps the clothing clause in gen-scene AND the clothed check in scene-regions; the check still demands a covered top and covered bottoms.
settings.setting: a big bright indoor swimming pool, turquoise water with lane ropes of red and white floats, a shallow end with wide steps going down into it, a curly yellow water slide splashing into the far corner, tall windows along one wall with daylight pouring across the water, white tiles, rippling reflections on the ceiling
settings.crowd: a lifeguard on a tall white chair with a whistle, swimmers doing lengths in the lanes, a parent in the shallow end with a toddler in armbands, a stack of foam kickboards by the wall, a big round clock, a swimming lesson of small children holding the side, rows of bleachers with towels and bags on them
settings.wardrobe: swimming clothes. Each child wears a swim shirt (a rash guard, short- or long-sleeved) on top and swim shorts or swimsuit bottoms below, in bright colours, a different combination each. Each child's hair keeps exactly its own colour, length and style — no swim caps, and no goggles over the face.

settings._comment: A HEADLINE setting (tools/scene-headlines.json): drawn only in a week with a trip on the calendar (vacation, flight, road trip) or a `scene:` note asking for one — hence "season": []. A grand old station rather than an airport: it reads as SETTING OFF for any kind of trip, and a station's crowd is a seek-and-find by nature.

settings.crowd: travellers with suitcases and hat boxes, a porter pushing a tall trolley of luggage, a family hugging goodbye, a conductor with a whistle, a pigeon on the clock, a kiosk selling pretzels, a newspaper stand, a stack of postcards, a lost umbrella, a guard waving a green flag
